Equivariant localizing motives and multiplicative norms on algebraic K-theory
Kaif Hilman and Maxime Ramzi

Abstract
. We construct multiplicative norms on equivariant nonconnective algebraic K K -theory for finite groups G G . We also construct a genuine equivariant version of THH equipped with a Dennis trace map from K-theory compatible with the multiplicative norms. To do so, we follow the general strategy of Blumberg–Gepner–Tabuada in the nonequivariant case by generalizing their category of localizing motives to the genuine equivariant context, building upon the theory of perfect G G -stable categories from [ Hil26 ] . Crucially, we proceed using the recent perspective on noncommutative motives from [ RSW25 ] which allows us to deal with non-exact functors on this category of motives. Together with an isotropy separation argument for equivariant cubes, we prove our main theorem that norms of stable categories preserve equivariant motivic equivalences. As an immediate consequence, we obtain a unique equivariant multiplicative refinement of nonconnective algebraic K K -theory. From these constructions and results, we draw several applications, namely: (1) that the endofunctor of (equivariant) tensor powers on ordinary perfect stable categories preserve motivic equivalences; (2) that the multiplicative norms also preserve the additive motivic equivalences, thus yielding a motivic refinement of a result of [ EH23 , CHL+24 ] that connective algebraic K-theory admits multiplicative norms; (3) we construct a genuine equivariant version of topological Hochschild homology equipped with a Dennis trace map that is compatible with multiplicative norms; and (4) we prove that every genuine G G -spectrum is the K-theory of a perfect G G -stable category.



1.
Introduction

Developments in recent decades have taught us that algebraic K-theory is best thought of as a homological invariant on stable categories, central to many parts of algebra, geometry, and topology. Just as in the algebraic topology of spaces where cohomological methods gain their full strength in large part from multiplicative structures such as cup products and Steenrod powers, algebraic K-theory finds its deepest results in connection with analogous multiplicative structures.
1
1

1

For example, see the positive solution of the chromatic redshift conjecture for
\mathbb{E}_{\infty}
–rings by
[
LMM+24
,
CMN+24
,
BSY22
]
or the new proof of Bökstedt periodicity using polynomial functoriality in
[
BGM+21
]
.
The fundamental result in service of guaranteeing such structures, which was proved in the seminal work by Blumberg-Gepner-Tabuada
[
BGT13
,
BGT14
]
on noncommutative motives, is that the algebraic K-theory functor
K\colon\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}\rightarrow\mathrm{Sp}
has a lax symmetric monoidal refinement. In particular, this enhances the spectrum
K({\mathcal{C}})
to an
\mathbb{E}_{\infty}
-ring spectrum when
{\mathcal{C}}
is a symmetric monoidal stable category. But even more than that, the motivic perspective of the aforementioned work endows K-theory with a universal property. For instance, this ensures all the desired multiplicative structures in probing K-theory via trace methods.

The goal of this paper is to extend this discussion to the setting of genuine equivariant stable homotopy theory for finite groups and capture the subtle multiplicative norm structures of Greenlees-May
[
GM97
]
and especially of the groundbreaking paper
[
HHR16
]
of Hill-Hopkins-Ravenel (cf. the introduction of
[
Hil26
]
for motivations for such structures, for example, in trying to prove completion theorems for K-theoretic objects). As we shall see, our equivariant work will have consequences also to the nonequivariant theory. For the sake of a leaner mathematical narrative, we have deferred explaining the connections to previous work on this subject in the literature to the end of the introduction.

1.1.
The main results

Let
G
be a finite group. There is no shortage in diversity as to what equivariant algebraic K-theory could mean.
2
2

2

See for example the end of the introduction in
[
Hil26
]
for a general lay of the land together with precise references.
For us, we will follow the interpretation of
[
BGS20
]
and mean by this the functor
\underline{{K}}\colon\mackey_{G}(\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}})\rightarrow\mathrm{Sp}_{G}\coloneqq\mackey_{G}(\mathrm{Sp})
obtained by taking
G
-Mackey functors
\mackey_{G}(-)
, in the sense of
[
Bar17
]
, of the
nonconnective
algebraic K-theory functor
K\colon\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}\rightarrow\mathrm{Sp}
.

In fact, in order to phrase the structure of equivariant multiplicative norms purely
\infty
-categorically, we will need to work in the more highly structured setting of categories parametrized over the orbit category
\mathcal{O}_{G}
of the group
G
as introduced by
[
BDG+16
,
Nar17
,
NS22
]
. In this setup, the basic objects are so-called
G
-categories
, which are objects
\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}=\{{\mathcal{C}}_{H}\}_{H\leq G}
in the category
\mathrm{Cat}_{G}\coloneqq\func(\mathcal{O}_{G}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat})
of
G
-categories. For the reader familiar with classical equivariant homotopy theory, this should indeed be viewed as a categorification of the notion of genuine
G
-spaces.

Moreover, as we shall recall in
Section

2
, there are also the equivariant analogues of stability and symmetric monoidal structures, termed unsurprisingly as
G
-stability and
G
-symmetric monoidal structures. For instance, just as a symmetric monoidal category is an object in
\cmonoid(\mathrm{Cat})
, the category of
\mathbb{E}_{\infty}
-monoids in categories, a
G
-symmetric monoidal category is an object in
\mackey_{G}(\mathrm{Cat})
, the
G
-Mackey functors in categories. The structures in the latter category should be thought of as an
\infty
-categorical axiomatization of the sorts of structures that were considered in
[
HHR16
]
. Intuitively, an object
\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}\in\mackey_{G}(\mathrm{Cat})
consists of the data of symmetric monoidal categories
{\mathcal{C}}_{H}
for each subgroup
H\leq G
, and additionally, for each inclusion of subgroups
H\leq K
, the datum of symmetric monoidal functors
\res^{K}_{H}\colon{\mathcal{C}}_{K}\rightarrow{\mathcal{C}}_{H}
and
\mathrm{N}^{K}_{H}\colon{\mathcal{C}}_{H}\rightarrow{\mathcal{C}}_{K}
called the restriction and multiplicative norm functors respectively, together with various compatibility coherences. The classical archetypal example to keep in mind here is the tensor induction in representation theory which takes a
H
-representation
V
and produces the
K
-representation
\bigotimes_{k\in K/H}kV
.

On the other hand, the notion of
G
-stability starts with “fiberwise” stability, namely the stability of each
{\mathcal{C}}_{H},H\leq G
, and is combined with
G
-semiadditivity. The latter notion axiomatizes the Wirthmüller isomorphism and is about admitting both induction and coinduction functors
{\mathcal{C}}_{H}\to{\mathcal{C}}_{G}
for each subgroup
H
, defined as left and right adjoints to the restriction functor respectively, and a certain canonical map between them being an equivalence. The first-named author proved in
[
Hil26
, Thm. B]
that these
G
-stable
G
-categories form a nonfull subcategory
\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}
of the category of
G
-Mackey functors of stable categories, where some previous notions of equivariant K-theory have been defined. These are in some sense the more natural/categorical Mackey functors, since their transfer structures arise from adjunctions rather than being abstract transfers. Furthermore, these in fact assemble to a
G
-symmetric monoidal
G
-category
\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}
.

Having sketched the general language, we now come to the contents of this article. The key insight in the recent work
[
RSW25
]
of the second-named author with Sosnilo and Winges is that the category of localizing motives as constructed by Blumberg-Gepner-Tabuada – which admits a universal property for mapping out of via colimit-preserving functors per construction – may alternatively be obtained by performing a Dwyer-Kan localization on the category
\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}
by inverting an appropriate notion of motivic equivalences.

One virtue of this observation is that the category of localizing motives admits a new universal property for mapping out of via not necessarily colimit-preserving functors. This opens up the possibility for constructing “power operations” at the level of localizing motives (which then descends to the level of algebraic K-theory by decategorification), and the main aim of the present work is to capitalise on this to deal with the multiplicative norms in the more refined setting of
G
-stable categories. In slightly more detail, we mimic
[
RSW25
]
and introduce an analogous notion of finitary
G
-localizing invariants on the
G
-category
\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}
, which in turn gives rise to a definition of
G
-motivic equivalences, cf.
3.1.4
. Using this, we then define the
G
-category
\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G}
as a Dwyer-Kan localization of
\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}
against the
G
-motivic equivalences. Our main results are then the following pair of theorems:

Theorem A

(cf.
3.2.1
)
.

Let
H\leq K
be an inclusion of subgroups of a finite group
G
. The multiplicative norm functor
\mathrm{N}_{H}^{K}:\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{H}\to\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{K}
sends
H
-motivic equivalences to
K
-motivic equivalences.

Theorem B

(cf.
3.1.13
,
3.2.2
,
3.3.1
and
3.3.3
)
.

The
G
-category
\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G}
is
G
-stable and
G
-presentable, and the Dwyer-Kan localization
\underline{{{\mathcal{U}}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}\colon\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\to\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G}
is the universal finitary
G
-localizing invariant. Moreover,
\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G}
attains a unique
G
-symmetric monoidal structure which refines
\underline{{{\mathcal{U}}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}
to a
G
-symmetric monoidal functor.

3

3

This provides one articulation of an answer to Problem 1.2 of Blumberg in
[
Lev
]
.

Among other things,
A
allows for a detailed analysis of operations related to motivic tensor powers in the nonequivariant setting, which we highlight below. Now, let us briefly comment on its proof. Just as in the nonequivariant setting, being a
G
-localizing invariant is defined in terms of sending Karoubi sequences (i.e. bifiber sequences) of
G
-categories to fiber sequences. Proving the theorem then essentially demands a study of how these exact sequences interact with the norm functors
\mathrm{N}^{K}_{H}
. The difficulty here is that these norms are not linear functors, and so applying it to Karoubi sequences produces null sequences in
\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}
which may fail to be either fiber or cofiber sequences – this is analogous to the module theoretic statement that if
A
is a sub-
R
-module of
B
, then
B^{\otimes_{R}n}/A^{\otimes_{R}n}
is not
(B/A)^{\otimes_{R}n}
.

To make matters worse, the leftmost term in these normed cofiber sequences involve colimits over equivariant cubes, which are significantly trickier to handle than ordinary cubes. For a more verbose discussion of these problems, we refer the reader to the introduction of
[
Hil26
]
.

The key techniques we develop to deal with these two problems, which might be of independent utility, are then certain isotropy separation arguments performed at the level of categories to check fully faithfulness, cf.
2.3.1
, as well as an equivariant cubical filtration, cf.
3.2.3
. These methods permits us to give inductive proofs for the relevant fully faithfulness statements as well as perform an equivariant cubical devissage to handle the cubical terms in the cofiber sequences above.

1.2.
Applications

We now turn to some consequences of the main results above. Our first application pertains to nonlinear operations on K-theory which features both in the question of polynomial functoriality of
K
-theory à la
[
BGM+21
]
and in questions of categorifying commutative ring spectra following
[
RSW25
]
. As an immediate consequence of
A
, we obtain the following, which is part of the theory of Borel localizing motives recorded in
Section

4.1
.

Corollary C

(cf.
4.1.4
)
.

Let
G
be a finite group and
X
a finite
G
-set. The functor
((-)^{\otimes X})_{hG}:\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}\to\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}
preserves motivic equivalences, and therefore induces an endofunctor of
\mathrm{Mot}^{\mathrm{loc}}
. In particular, for any natural number
n
,
((-)^{\otimes n})_{h\Sigma_{n}}
preserves motivic equivalences, and therefore, the functor
\Gamma_{n}
introduced in
[
BGM+21
, Cons. 4.16]
also preserves motivic equivalences, and induces an endofunctor of
\mathrm{Mot}^{\mathrm{loc}}
.

From the latter part of this statement, one can in fact directly recover the main theorem of
[
BGM+21
]
which extends the functoriality of the connective algebraic K-theory space functor to polynomial functors between stable categories, refining to the level of spaces many of the classical nonadditive operations on the K-theory groups.

Before moving on to the next application, let us explain the essential content of this result and its proof. In the body of the paper, we will in fact prove something slightly stronger, i.e. that
(-)^{\otimes X}\colon\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}\rightarrow\func(BG,\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}})
sends motivic equivalences to
Borel
motivic equivalences, i.e. those morphisms which are inverted by all localizing invariants out of
\func(BG,\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}})
. Importantly, note that there are localizing invariants out of
\func(BG,\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}})
which do not factor through the forgetful functor to
\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}
, for instance, the functor
K((-)_{hG})
. So even though the notion of Karoubi sequences in both
\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}
and
\func(BG,\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}})
only depend on the underlying sequence in
\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}
, Borel motivic equivalences in
\func(BG,\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}})
are
not
checked by passing to the underlying morphism in
\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}
.

From the point of view of giving a proof to such results, the reason it is not as straightforward as one might first surmise is the following: for two motivic equivalences
f\colon\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}
and
f^{\prime}\colon\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}^{\prime}
in
\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}
, the easy reason that
f\otimes f^{\prime}
is also a motivic equivalence is that we can factor it as
(f\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{B}^{\prime}})\circ(\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{A}}\otimes f^{\prime})
. In turn, it is easy to show that both
(f\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{B}^{\prime}}),(\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{A}}\otimes f^{\prime})
are motivic equivalences because the tensor product preserves Karoubi sequences in each variable. However, in the equivariant context, one needs rather to argue that morphisms like
f^{\otimes G}\colon\mathcal{A}^{\otimes G}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}^{\otimes G}
are (Borel) motivic equivalences. In this situation, the currying trick from before of factorizing the morphism fails because the factorization is not through
G
-equivariant morphisms, i.e. they are not morphisms in
\func(BG,\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}})
. This is the fundamental reason which necessitates a symmetric way of dealing with the problem via cubes as afforded by
A
.

Coming back to the genuine equivariant situation, notice that the main theorems have been about nonconnective algebraic K-theory, and one can also wonder about similar questions for the connective variant thereof or rather its associated category of motives. In this setting, the appropriate version of excision is the weaker requirement of being a
G
-splitting
4
4

4

Traditionally, splitting invariants are called additive invariants. We have opted to follow this new terminology from
[
RSW25
]
, see their Remark 6.4 for a justification.
invariant (
4.2.2
) rather than a
G
-localizing invariant. For this question, we use that nonconnective K-theory is a
G
-lax symmetric monoidal functor by
B
and deduce the following connective analogue:

Theorem D

(cf.
4.2.8
)
.

There is a
G
-category
\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{split},\mathrm{abs}}_{G}
which is
G
-additive, equipped with a map
\underline{{{\mathcal{U}}}}^{\mathrm{split},\mathrm{abs}}\colon\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\to\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{split},\mathrm{abs}}_{G}
witnessing it as the universal
G
-splitting invariant. Moreover,
\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{split},\mathrm{abs}}_{G}
attains a unique
G
-symmetric monoidal structure which refines
\underline{{{\mathcal{U}}}}^{\mathrm{split},\mathrm{abs}}
to a
G
-symmetric monoidal functor.

Finally, equivariant connective K-theory
\underline{{K}}^{\mathrm{cn}}\colon\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\subset\underline{{\mackey}}_{G}(\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}})\xrightarrow{\underline{{K}}^{\mathrm{cn}}}\mathchoice{\mbox{\uline{\phantom{$\displaystyle\mathrm{Sp}$}}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.19133pt\raisebox{-0.46193pt}[0.0pt]{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{Sp}$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.35355pt\raisebox{-0.35355pt}[0.0pt]{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{Sp}$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.46193pt\raisebox{-0.19133pt}[0.0pt]{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{Sp}$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.5pt\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt]{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{Sp}$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.46193pt\raisebox{0.19133pt}[0.0pt]{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{Sp}$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.35355pt\raisebox{0.35355pt}[0.0pt]{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{Sp}$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.19133pt\raisebox{0.46193pt}[0.0pt]{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{Sp}$}\hss}\mbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{Sp}$}}}}_{G}
. In particular for any
G
-
\infty
-operad
\mathcal{O}
and any
\mathbb{E}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{O}
-ring
G
-spectrum
R
, the Dennis trace map
K_{G}(R)\to\mathrm{THH}_{G}(R)
can be canonically upgraded to an
\mathcal{O}
-ring map.

We expect this to be a useful fundamental piece of structural theory when running a trace method argument in the equivariant setting in the same way that having the structure of a ring map on the Dennis trace is an indispensable part of the nonequivariant story. As an illustration that the
G
-lax symmetric monoidality of the trace map potentially captures interesting and nontrivial structures, we note in
Example

4.3.11
that for every finite group
G
, the usual trace map
K(\mathbb{S})\rightarrow\mathrm{THH}(\mathbb{S})=\mathbb{S}
admits a factorization
K(\mathbb{S})\rightarrow\Phi^{G}\underline{{K}}(\mathbb{S}_{G})\rightarrow\mathrm{THH}(\mathbb{S})=\mathbb{S}
where
\Phi^{G}
is the geometric fixed point functor. As further examples, we also point out lifts of the proper Tate construction on the Dennis trace along the Nikolaus–Scholze Tate–Frobenius map in two situations in
Examples

4.3.12
and
4.3.13
.

As complements to this construction of equivariant THH, we also provide several basic formal properties about it, for example, that it interacts nicely with geometric fixed points and that it is computed as a free loop space when applied to equivariant local systems. We also use it to split off the
G
-suspension spectrum of a
G
-space from a version of equivariant A-theory, which we expect to coincide with the one of Malkiewich–Merling
[
MM22
]
.

Finally, we forget all matters about multiplicative norms and give an application of the mere construction of the category of equivariant localizing motives and the Dennis trace map from
E
. Namely, with all the machinery set up, we may directly copy the proof of
[
RSW25
, Thm. 1.6]
to obtain the following genuine equivariant generalization of the main theorem of
[
RSW24
]
that every spectrum is the algebraic K-theory of some stable category.

Theorem F

(cf.
4.4.1
)
.

Let
X\in\mathrm{Sp}_{G}
. Then there exists
\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}
and an equivalence
\underline{{K}}(\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}})\simeq X\in\mathrm{Sp}_{G}
.

One might be tempted to try to
deduce
the statement above from the nonequivariant result as follows: in
[
RSW24
]
, it was shown that in fact
K\colon\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}\rightarrow\mathrm{Sp}
admits a functorial section
s
, and so one could try to deduce that this induces also a functorial section to
K\colon\mackey_{G}(\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}})\rightarrow\mackey_{G}(\mathrm{Sp})=\mathrm{Sp}_{G}
. However, the functor
s
in fact does
not
preserve finite products, and so it does not induce a functor backwards on Mackey functors. As such, it seems to us necessary to set up the theory of equivariant localizing motives in order to obtain
F
. Moreover, the theorem above also gives a stronger conclusion since it asserts that every genuine
G
-spectrum may be realised as the K–theory spectrum of an object in the nonfull subcategory
\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\subset\mackey_{G}(\mathrm{Sp})
.

1.3.
Relation to other work

We only mention here the types of equivariant K-theory that are most directly related to what we consider in this paper. For a survey of other kinds of equivariant K-theory, see for example the introduction to
[
Hil26
]
.

As far as we are aware, the first work to construct the multiplicative norms on algebraic K-theory is Elmanto-Haugseng
[
EH23
, Thm. 4.3.7]
. More specifically, using the formalism of bispans and taking the deep work on polynomial functoriality of K-theory by Barwick-Glasman-Mathew-Nikolaus
[
BGM+21
]
as the K-theoretic input, they enhanced the equivariant algebraic K-theory
space
with the structure of multiplicative norms. Later on, Cnossen–Haugseng–Lenz–Linskens
[
CHL+24
, Thm. B]
proved an abstract result about product-preserving presheaves on bispans of finite
G
-sets which enhances Elmanto-Haugseng’s construction from the K-theory space to the connective K-theory
spectrum
.

In a separate vein, the first-named author
[
Hil26
]
enhanced the connective algebraic K-theory spectrum with the structure of multiplicative norms in the special case of finite 2-groups directly without recourse to
[
BGM+21
]
. The approach there is to construct the
G
-category of equivariant splitting motives and perform an explicit equivariant cubical analysis in the case of
G=C_{2}
. The present work therefore finds its precursor in
[
Hil26
]
and completes the approach therein. Just as in
loc. cit.
, our approach does
not
depend on
[
BGM+21
]
and can, in fact, essentially reprove this result. However, unlike
loc. cit.
, our main object of study are equivariant
localizing
motives and
nonconnective
K-theory, which as far as we know, has not been treated before. We then use our knowledge in the nonconnective setting to deduce the connective version also. Furthermore, by constructing the category of localizing motives, we place the story in the context of universal properties and thus allows us, among other things, to view the equivariant Dennis trace map as a normed map.

Since we mentioned that we could use our methods to construct an equivariant Dennis trace, we also note that
[
CGK25
]
already constructed an equivariant Dennis trace at the point-set level. However, their Dennis trace has target Borel equivariant
\mathrm{THH}
as opposed to the genuine equivariant
\underline{{\mathrm{THH}}}
mentioned in
E
. It would be beneficial to clarify the relationship between our construction and their work
6
6

6

They write “…this approach does not refine all the way to a map of genuine G-spectra. Since the equivariant algebraic K-theory of a G-ring spectrum depends only on the category of perfect modules over the underlying ring with G-action”, which is certainly not the case for our version of equivariant algebraic
K
-theory.
. We also mention that, in forthcoming work, Mark Gotliboym will also give a different construction of the equivariant Dennis trace map and also treat equivariant cyclotomic structures, which we do not do here.

Finally, in the operator algebraic context, we were informed by Julian Kranz that Ulrich Bunke proved a result analogous to
B
in the context of
C^{*}
-algebras and operator
K
-theory, see
[
Bun23
, Prop. 2.19]
(a precursor of this can also be found in Izumi’s
[
Izu17
, Theorem 2.1]
). The results of
[
RSW25
]
are what allow us to do similar kinds of arguments in the categorical context as in the
C^{*}
-algebraic context, where the KK-category has been known to be a Dwyer–Kan localization of the category of certain
C^{*}
-algebras for a longer time.

1.4.
Organization of the paper

We lay out the parametrized language and ingredients needed in
Section

2
. After recalling and recording some basic elements in
Section

2.1
, including the equivariant cubes, we recall in
Section

2.2
the notion of
G
-perfect-stable categories from
[
Hil26
]
as well as the categorical isotropy separation from
[
HKK24
]
. With this latter construction, we provide an isotropy separation principle to check fully faithfulness in
Section

2.3
.

Next, we begin our K-theoretic work proper in
Section

3
. We define the
G
-category of
G
-lozalizing motives in
Section

3.1
and prove a Blumberg–Gepner–Tabuada-style universal property in
3.1.13
. We then come to the heart of the article in
Section

3.2
where we prove
A
by performing various cubical isotropy separation arguments. Following that, we show in
Section

3.3
that equivariant nonconnective K-theory is corepresented by the unit in equivariant localizing motives, and thus complete the proof of
B
.

In
Section

4
, we provide four applications of the preceding results. Using
A
, we consider a variant called Borel localizing motives in
Section

4.1
and prove
C
. We then consider
G
-splitting motives in
Section

4.2
and prove
D
pertaining to
connective
equivariant algebraic K-theory. In
Section

4.3
, we construct an equivariant THH and use our main theorem to construct a normed Dennis trace map as in
E
. Lastly, we prove
F
that every genuine
G
-spectrum is the K-theory of some
G
-stable category in
Section

4.4
.

We end our work with four technical appendices which might be of independent interest. In
Appendix

A
, we supply an adjunction needed to prove the useful adjunction
2.1.12
relating equivariant semiadditive categories and nonequivariant semiadditive categories via the Mackey functor construction. In
Appendix

B
, we prove the general utility
B.0.1
which says that in the presentable setting, a
G
-stable category is equivalently given by a
\mathrm{Sp}_{G}
-module in ordinary categories. We then show that finite posets with
G
-actions are equivariantly finite in
Appendix

C
, which is important in the general equivariant theory to insure that norms preserve equivariant compactness. For example, this is crucial
7
7

7

See the end of the introduction in
[
Hil26
]
for more details on how this fits into the general foundations.
in constructing a
G
-symmetric monoidal structure on
\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}
. Finally, we construct a 2-categorical enhancement of the
G
-symmetric monoidal structure on presentables in
Appendix

D
needed for our construction of equivariant THH.

2.
Elements

2.1.
Preliminaries

The basic materials here belong to the general theory of
parametrized category theory
as introduced by Barwick-Dotto-Glasman-Nardin-Shah. As such, we refer the reader to
[
BDG+16
,
Sha23
,
Sha22
,
Nar16
,
Nar17
,
NS22
]
for the source materials. The reader may also find
[
Hil26
, §2.1 and 2.2]
a convenient reference for a detailed collection of the materials we will need in this work together with precise citations to the aforementioned body of work. As such, we will adopt a brisk pace in the coming recollections. The reader familiar with parametrized category theory should skip ahead to
Section

3
and return here as needed. We mention also that there is a more recent alternative, and in many (but not all) ways more general, treatment of parametrized category theory via topos theory due to Martini-Wolf, cf.
[
Mar22a
,
Mar22
,
MW24
,
MW25
]
. We have opted to use the older theory since it is the one which affords the notions of
G
-stability and
G
-symmetric monoidality, both of which play a central role in the present work.

G
-categories and
G
-symmetric monoidality

Let
G
be a finite group throughout the article.

Recollections 2.1.1

(
G
-categories)
.

As in the introduction, the category
\mathrm{Cat}_{G}
of
G
-categories is defined as
\func(\mathcal{O}_{G}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat})
where
\mathcal{O}_{G}
is the orbit category of
G
. We denote a generic object therein by
\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
, and for
H\leq G
, we write
{\mathcal{C}}_{H}=\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}(G/H)\in\mathrm{Cat}
for its evaluation at
G/H
.

In fact, these categories assemble across the subgroups of
G
to yield a large
G
-category
\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}_{G}\in\widehat{\mathrm{Cat}}_{G}\coloneqq\func(\mathcal{O}_{G}^{\mathrm{op}},\widehat{\mathrm{Cat}})
of small
G
-categories which sends
G/H
to
\mathrm{Cat}_{H}
, and for an inclusion
w\colon H\rightarrowtail K
of subgroups of
G
, the restriction functor
w^{*}\colon\mathrm{Cat}_{K}\rightarrow\mathrm{Cat}_{H}
is induced by the forgetful functor
w\colon\mathcal{O}_{H}\simeq(\mathcal{O}_{K})_{/K/H}\rightarrow\mathcal{O}_{K}
. These functors admit left and right adjoints
w_{!}
and
w_{*}
, respectively. They should be viewed as indexed coproducts and indexed products, i.e. coproducts and products indexed over (finite)
G
-sets instead of just over (finite) sets; or alternatively as induction and coinduction functors. Moreover, since
\mathrm{Cat}_{G}
is cartesian closed, there are internal functor categories which we denote by
\underline{{\func}}(-,-)
. For
\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}},\underline{{{\mathcal{D}}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{G}
and
f\colon G/H\rightarrow G/G
the unique map, evaluation of
\underline{{\func}}(\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}},\underline{{{\mathcal{D}}}})
at
G/H
yields the category
\func_{H}(f^{*}\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}},f^{*}\underline{{{\mathcal{D}}}})
of
H
-functors from
f^{*}\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
to
f^{*}\underline{{{\mathcal{D}}}}
.

In fact, we can (and it is convenient to be able to) speak also of
V
-categories for any finite
G
-set
V=\coprod_{i}G/H_{i}
as follows: via the fully faithful inclusion
\mathcal{O}_{G}\subseteq\mathrm{Fin}_{G}
into all finite
G
-sets, we may consider the slice category
(\mathcal{O}_{G})_{/V}\simeq\coprod_{i}(\mathcal{O}_{G})_{/G/H_{i}}
and therefore also
\mathrm{Cat}_{V}\coloneqq\func((\mathcal{O}_{G})_{/V}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat})\simeq\prod_{i}\mathrm{Cat}_{H_{i}}
. Restricting along the forgetful map
(\mathcal{O}_{G})_{/V}\rightarrow\mathcal{O}_{G}
, we obtain a restriction functor
V^{*}\colon\mathrm{Cat}_{G}\rightarrow\mathrm{Cat}_{V}
, so that for a
G
-category
\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{G}
,
V^{*}\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{V}
will denote its associated
V
-category.

Terminology 2.1.2
.

The notion of
G
-categories recalled above is more highly structured than merely being a category with
G
-actions. The latter notion does however embed in the former via the inclusion
b_{*}\colon\func(BG,\mathrm{Cat})\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Cat}_{G}
given by right Kan extending along the fully faithful inclusion
b\colon BG\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{G}
of the full subcategory spanned by
G/e\in\mathcal{O}_{G}
. Following standard parlance, we will sometimes refer to an object in
\mathrm{Cat}_{G}
as a
genuine
equivariant category and an object in
\func(BG,\mathrm{Cat})
as a
Borel
equivariant category, and extend the use of these adjectives to other situations where a similar distinction makes sense.

Recollections 2.1.3

(Adjunctions and (co)limits)
.

Since
\mathrm{Cat}_{G}=\func(\mathcal{O}_{G}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat})
is naturally an
(\infty,2)
-category, we may speak of adjunctions. It turns out that a
G
-functor has a left (resp. right) adjoint if and only if it has one levelwise and all the associated Beck–Chevalley squares commute (and in this case, the right, resp. left, adjoint is given by the levelwise adjoint).

For
G
-categories
\underline{{I}}
and
\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
, we say that
\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
admits
\underline{{I}}
-indexed colimits (resp. limits) if the restriction
G
-functor
I^{*}\colon\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\func}}(\underline{{I}},\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}})
admits a left adjoint
I_{!}
(resp. right adjoint
I_{*}
) in
\mathrm{Cat}_{G}
. More generally, we can of course also speak of left/right Kan extensions along a map
\underline{{I}}\rightarrow\underline{{J}}
of
G
-categories. An important special case is when we consider a map
w\colon W\rightarrow V
in
\mathrm{Fin}_{G}
as a map
w\colon\underline{{W}}\rightarrow\underline{{V}}
of
G
-categories. We say that
\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
admits finite indexed coproducts (resp. products) if
w_{!}
(resp.
w_{*}
) exists for all such
w
. In these cases, note also that
\underline{{\func}}(\underline{{W}},\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}})\simeq W_{*}W^{*}\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
, and for example when
V=G/G
, the restriction map
w^{*}\colon\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}\rightarrow W_{*}W^{*}\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
should be thought of as the equivariant diagonal map into the equivariant product
W_{*}
.

For
I\in\mathrm{Cat}
, we say that
\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
admits (fiberwise)
I
-indexed (co)limits if it admits
\underline{{\operatorname{const}}}I
-indexed (co)limits. It turns out that this is equivalent to requiring that
{\mathcal{C}}_{H}
admits
I
-indexed (co)limits for each
H\leq G
, and that all the restriction functors preserve these.

We say that a
G
-category is
G
-cocomplete (resp.
G
-complete) if it admits left (resp. right) Kan extensions along
G
-functors
\underline{{I}}\rightarrow\underline{{V}}
where
\underline{{V}}\in\mathrm{Fin}_{G}
. A practically useful equivalent characterisation of this is that the
G
-category admits fiberwise colimits (resp. limits) and admits finite indexed coproducts (resp. products).

Recollections 2.1.4

(Ind-completions and idempotent-completeness)
.

The notion of compact objects in a parametrized category is simply given by being fiberwise compact, cf.
[
Hil24
, §5.1]
.
The parametrized Ind-completion functor which freely adds (fiberwise) filtered colimits is simply given by performing fiberwise Ind-completions, cf.
[
Sha22
]
. Furthermore, we say that a
G
-category is idempotent-complete if it is so fiberwise, cf.
[
Hil24
, Def. 5.3.1]
.

Recollections 2.1.5

(
G
-presentability)
.

There is a good theory of
G
-presentable categories by
[
Hil24
,
MW25
]
and it is much the same as in the ordinary world, for instance, there is the adjoint functor theorem in this context, cf. for example
[
Hil24
, Thm. 6.2.1]
. The
G
-presentable
G
-categories may be characterised as those
G
-categories which are
G
-cocomplete and which are fiberwise presentable, cf. for example
[
Hil24
, Thm. 6.1.2 (7)]
.

Recollections 2.1.6

(
G
-symmetric monoidal structures)
.

Just as in the nonequivariant situation where a symmetric monoidal category is equivalently described, cf.
[
NS22
, Thm. 2.3.9]
, as a finite-product-preserving functor from spans of finite sets to categories, a
G
-symmetric monoidal category is a
G
-Mackey functor valued in categories, i.e. an object
\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}^{\otimes}
in
\mackey_{G}(\mathrm{Cat})\coloneqq\func^{\times}(\spancategory(\mathrm{Fin}_{G}),\mathrm{Cat})
where the right hand side denotes the category of finite-product-preserving functors from the span category of
\mathrm{Fin}_{G}
to
\mathrm{Cat}
. Such objects carry a lot of structures, which includes an underlying
G
-category
\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
. For any map
w\colon W\rightarrow V
in
\mathrm{Fin}_{G}
, the restriction functoriality
w^{*}\colon{\mathcal{C}}_{V}\rightarrow{\mathcal{C}}_{W}
is endowed with a symmetric monoidal structure; furthermore, there are also symmetric monoidal functors
w_{\otimes}\colon{\mathcal{C}}_{W}\rightarrow{\mathcal{C}}_{V}
which generalize the tensor products in the nonequivariant setting, to be thought of as the structure of tensors indexed by finite
G
-sets and which we shall refer to as the
multiplicative norms
from now on.

Example 2.1.7
.

Since the
G
-category
\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}_{G}
admits indexed products, it may be endowed with the (unique)
G
-cartesian symmetric monoidal structure, cf.
[
Ste25
, Thm. A’]
.

There are infinite coherences governing the interaction between the restriction on the one hand and the indexed products and multiplicative norms on the other hand. The fundamental basechange
8
8

8

classically, these are also known as double-coset formulas.
relations are the following, which notations we will refer to throughout the article.

Setting 2.1.8
.

The following are the standard pullback diagrams in
\mathrm{Fin}_{G}

or

When necessary, we write
Z=\coprod_{i}Z_{i}
for the orbital decomposition of
Z
and also write
\overline{u}=\sqcup_{i}\overline{u}_{i}
and

for the associated decomposition.

G
-semiadditivity and
G
-stability

Next, we recall Nardin’s
[
Nar16
]
definition of
G
-semiadditive and
G
-stable
G
-categories.

Recollections 2.1.9

(
G
-semiadditivity)
.

Let
\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{G}
be a pointed
G
-category, i.e. by virtue of the notion of fiberwise (co)limits from
2.1.3
, this means that
{\mathcal{C}}_{H}
is a pointed category for each
H\leq G
, and the restriction functors preserve the zero objects. Suppose also that it admits finite indexed (co)products. Then, as in the nonequivariant situation, for each map
w\colon W\rightarrow V
in
\mathrm{Fin}_{G}
, there is a Beck-Chevalley-type transformation
w_{!}\Rightarrow w_{*}
of functors
\underline{{\func}}(\underline{{W}},\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}})\rightarrow\underline{{\func}}(\underline{{V}},\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}})
using the pointedness assumption. We say that
\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
is
G
-semiadditive if all these transformations are equivalences.

Using this, we may then define Nardin’s notion of
G
-stability.

Definition 2.1.10
.

Let
\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}\in\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}
. We say that it is
G
-stable if it is fiberwise stable, that is, each
{\mathcal{C}}_{H}
is stable, and it is
G
-semiadditive.

Example 2.1.11
.

The property of
G
-stability axiomatizes the basic structures in genuine equivariant stable homotopy theory. As such, the basic examples of
G
-stable categories include that of genuine equivariant spectra

There is a general way of relating ordinary functors and
G
-functors in the semiadditive regime which is useful to connect equivariant statements to ordinary, nonequivariant ones. Since the proof requires some general technical inputs, we have chosen to defer the proof to the end of

Proposition 2.1.12
.

There is an adjunction

(-)^{G}:\mathrm{Cat}^{\oplus}_{G}\rightleftarrows\mathrm{Cat}^{\oplus}:\underline{{\mackey}}_{G}(-)

between the category of
G
-semiadditive
G
-categories and the category of semiadditive categories, where
(-)^{G}
is the functor which evaluates a
G
-category at level
G/G
, and
\underline{{\mackey}}_{G}(-)
sends an ordinary semiadditive category
\mathcal{A}
to the
G
-category which at level
G/H
is given by the
\mathcal{A}
-valued
H
-Mackey functors, i.e.
\mackey_{H}(\mathcal{A})\coloneqq\func^{\times}(\spancategory(\mathrm{Fin}_{H}),\mathcal{A})
, the category of finite-product-preserving from the span category of
\mathrm{Fin}_{H}
to
\mathcal{A}
.

The counit is given by the fixed point functor
\mackey_{G}({\mathcal{C}})\xrightarrow{(-)^{G}}{\mathcal{C}}
, and for
\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{G}^{\oplus}
and
K\leq H\leq G
, the composite
\mathcal{A}_{H}\xrightarrow{\textnormal{unit}^{H}}\mackey_{H}(\mathcal{A}_{G})\xrightarrow{(-)^{K}}\mathcal{A}_{G}
is given by
\coind^{G}_{K}\res^{H}_{K}\simeq\mathrm{Ind}_{K}^{G}\res_{K}^{H}
.

G
-distributivity

Equivariant distributivity is a notion which generalizes the idea of tensor products which are bicocontinuous into the equivariant setting. This was first defined by Nardin in his thesis
[
Nar17
]
, but see also
[
NS22
, Def. 3.2.3]
where the theory was further developed. This concept will play a central role in our main results and we recall it now.

Definition 2.1.13
.

Let
w\colon W\rightarrow V
be a map in
\mathrm{Fin}_{G}
. A
V
-functor
w_{*}\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}\rightarrow\underline{{{\mathcal{D}}}}
is said to be
w
-
distributive
if for any map
u\colon U\rightarrow V
in
\mathrm{Fin}_{G}
and using the notations as in the pullback square (i) in
2.1.8
, and a
Z
-colimit diagram
\partial\colon\underline{K}^{\triangleright}\rightarrow\overline{u}^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
, the diagram

(\overline{w}_{*}\underline{K})^{\triangleright}\xlongrightarrow{\mathrm{can}}\overline{w}_{*}(\underline{K}^{\triangleright})\xlongrightarrow{\overline{w}_{*}\partial}\overline{w}_{*}\overline{u}^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\simeq u^{*}{w}_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\xlongrightarrow{u^{*}\partial}{u}^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}

is a
U
–colimit diagram in
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
.

This allows us to define the equivariant analogue of distributive symmetric monoidal structures.

Definition 2.1.14
.

Let
\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
be a
G

-category. A

is said to be a
distributive
G
-symmetric monoidal structure
if for all maps
w\colon W\rightarrow V
in
\mathrm{Fin}_{G}
, the
V
-functor
w_{\otimes}\colon w_{*}w^{*}V^{*}\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}\rightarrow V^{*}\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
is
w
-distributive.

We will mainly be concerned with the interactions of distributive multiplicative norms with two kinds of colimits, namely filtered colimits and cofiber sequences. We record these now.

Remark 2.1.16
.

Let
I\in\mathrm{Cat}
be a sifted category. Then note that the constant
G
-category
\underline{{\operatorname{const}}}I
satisfies an equivariant siftedness property, i.e. for every map
w\colon W\rightarrow V
in
\mathrm{Fin}_{G}
, the diagonal
V
-functor
\Delta\colon\underline{{\operatorname{const}}}I\rightarrow w_{*}w^{*}\underline{{\operatorname{const}}}I
is
G
-colimit cofinal. This is because
\Delta
is given fiberwise by the usual diagonal functor of
I
to a finite product of itself, and equivariant colimit cofinality is checked fiberwise by
[
Sha23
, Thm. 6.7]
.

Observation 2.1.17
.

Let
\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
be a
G
-cocomplete
G
-category equipped with a distributive
G
–symmetric monoidal structure and
w\colon W\rightarrow V
a map in
\mathrm{Fin}_{G}
. Then the functor
w_{\otimes}\colon{\mathcal{C}}_{W}\rightarrow{\mathcal{C}}_{V}
given by the
G
-symmetric monoidal structure preserves sifted colimits. To see this, given any sifted colimit diagram
I^{\triangleright}\rightarrow{\mathcal{C}}_{W}
, we get an induced
G
-colimit diagram
\underline{{\operatorname{const}}}I^{\triangleright}\rightarrow W^{*}\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
. Hence, by distributivity, the diagram
(w_{*}\underline{{\operatorname{const}}}I)^{\triangleright}\rightarrow w_{*}(\underline{{\operatorname{const}}}I^{\triangleright})\rightarrow w_{*}w^{*}V^{*}\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}\xrightarrow{w_{\otimes}}V^{*}\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
is a
G
-colimit diagram. Thus, by
2.1.16
, so is the restricted diagram
\underline{{\operatorname{const}}}I^{\triangleright}\xrightarrow{\Delta}(w_{*}\underline{{\operatorname{const}}}I)^{\triangleright}\rightarrow w_{*}(\underline{{\operatorname{const}}}I^{\triangleright})\rightarrow w_{*}w^{*}V^{*}\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}\xrightarrow{w_{\otimes}}V^{*}\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
. Evaluating this composite
V
-functor at level
V
now gives the desired conclusion.

The case of cofiber sequences is a bit trickier to deal with. To properly deal with these, we will need to recall the notion of equivariant cubes. Model categorical precursors to our considerations here have appeared for example in
[
HHR16
, App. A.3]
and in
[
Dot17
]
. However, many point-set arguments there do not work directly in the fully
\infty
-categorical context; we provide model-independent and more general arguments for the next two lemmas, building on the
\infty
-categorical treatment in
[
Hil26
, §3]
.

Recollections 2.1.18

(Equivariant cubes)
.

Let
w\colon W\rightarrow V
be a map in
\mathrm{Fin}_{G}
. We then obtain a
V
-category
w_{*}[1]\in\mathrm{Cat}_{V}
by applying the indexed product functor
w_{*}\colon\mathrm{Cat}_{W}\rightarrow\mathrm{Cat}_{V}
on the constant
W
-category
[1]
. These are fiberwise given by cubes of various dimensions, cf.
[
Hil26
, Prop. 3.1.2]
. Moreover, they are in fact even equivariantly finite categories by
C.0.1
.

In the special case of the unique map
w\colon W\rightarrow G/G
in
\mathrm{Fin}_{G}
, it is easy to describe
w_{*}[1]\in\mathrm{Cat}_{G}
concretely: it may equivalently be viewed as the
G
-category of subsets of the finite
G
-set
W
which at level
K\leq G
is given by the full subposet of subsets of
W
which are
K
-invariant under the action of
K
on
W
.

The following result is the first technical result we need regarding the interaction of norms and cofibers – it gives us a specific way of understanding the norm of the cofiber of a map
x\to y
in terms of
x
and
y
.

Lemma 2.1.19
.

Let
\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
be a pointed
W
-category and
\underline{{{\mathcal{D}}}}
a be pointed
V
-category, with finite
W
-, resp.
V
-colimits, and let
w\colon W\rightarrow V
be a map in
\mathrm{Fin}_{G}
. Let
N\colon w_{*}\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}\to\underline{{{\mathcal{D}}}}
an
w
-distributive functor and
x\to y\to z
a cofiber sequence in
\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
. The induced maps fit in a cofiber sequence

\mathop{colim}\displaylimits_{w_{*}[1]\setminus 1}N(x\rightarrow y)\longrightarrow N(y)\rightarrow N(z)

where we have written
N(x\rightarrow y)
for the functor
w_{*}[1]\xrightarrow{w_{*}(x\rightarrow y)}w_{*}\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}\xrightarrow{N}\underline{{{\mathcal{D}}}}
.

Proof.

The proof works exactly as in
[
Hil26
, Prop. 3.2.8]
where the case of
N
being part of a parametrized symmetric monoidal structure was treated. Here, we just replace the statement that tensoring with zero objects gives the zero object with the fact that distributive multivariable functors evaluate to zero when one of the inputs is the zero object.
∎

The following cubical filtration will serve as the combinatorial backbone of our main result.

Notation 2.1.20
.

Let
w\colon G/H\rightarrow G/G
be the unique map in
\mathrm{Fin}_{G}
. Viewing
w_{*}[1]
as the
G
-category of subsets of
G/H
, we write
(w_{*}[1])_{\leq i}\subseteq w_{*}[1]
for the full
G
-subcategory of subsets of size at most
i
where
1\leq i\leq|G/H|
.

Lemma 2.1.21
.

Let
\underline{{{\mathcal{D}}}}
be a be pointed
G
-category with finite
G
-colimits,
w\colon G/H\rightarrow G/G
be the unique map, and let
F\colon w_{*}[1]\rightarrow\underline{{{\mathcal{D}}}}
be a diagram. For every
1\leq i\leq|G/H|
, the map

\mathop{colim}\displaylimits_{{(w_{*}[1])}_{\leq i-1}\backslash 1}F\longrightarrow\mathop{colim}\displaylimits_{{(w_{*}[1])}_{\leq i}\backslash 1}F

has cofiber given by a finite coproduct of properly induced objects in
\underline{{{\mathcal{D}}}}
.

Dwyer-Kan localizations

We now explain some equivariant aspects of Dwyer-Kan localizations. As usual, this is the procedure by which we formally invert arrows belonging to a wide subcategory, to be thought of as the “weak equivalences” in the classical setting of model categories. It turns out that it is given in a fiberwise fashion on a
V
-category for any
V\in\mathrm{Fin}_{G}
, cf. for example the proof of
[
Hil26
, Prop. 2.3.4]
.

Recollections 2.1.22

(Symmetric monoidality)
.

Let
T\in\mathrm{Fin}_{G}
,
\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
be a
T
-symmetric monoidal category, and
\underline{{S}}\subseteq\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
a wide
T
-subcategory. Suppose that
\underline{{S}}
is closed under the multiplicative norms, i.e. for all morphisms
w\colon W\rightarrow V
in
(\mathrm{Fin}_{G})_{/V}
and all morphisms
f\colon x\rightarrow y
in
S_{W}
, the morphism
w_{\otimes}f\colon w_{\otimes}x\rightarrow w_{\otimes}y
is in
S_{V}
. Then by
[
Hil26
, Prop. 2.3.4]
, we see that the Dwyer-Kan localization
\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}\rightarrow\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}[\underline{{S}}^{-1}]
naturally refines to a
V
-symmetric monoidal functor.

Next, we show that Dwyer-Kan localizations interact nicely with semiadditivity.

Lemma 2.1.23
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}
be a
G
-category, and
\underline{{S}}\subset\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}
a wide
G
-subcategory. If
\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}
admits finite indexed coproducts and
\underline{{S}}
is stable under those, then
\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}[\underline{{S}}^{-1}]
admits finite indexed coproducts and the localization functor preserves them. Furthermore, if
\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}
is
G
-semiadditive, then so is
\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}[\underline{{S}}^{-1}]
. Finally, if
F\colon\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}\rightarrow\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
preserves finite indexed coproducts and sends
\underline{{W}}
to equivalences, then the unique factorization
\overline{F}\colon\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}[\underline{{S}}^{-1}]\rightarrow\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
also preserves finite indexed coproducts.

Proof.

Let
w\colon W\rightarrow V
be a map in
\mathrm{Fin}_{G}
. By basechanging first to
V
-categories if necessary, we may without loss of generality assume that
V=G/G
. Recall from
2.1.3
that
\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}
admits
W
-indexed coproducts is equivalent to the diagonal functor
\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}\to W_{*}W^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}
admitting a left adjoint. If this left adjoint preserves
w_{*}\underline{{S}}
, then it descends to the localization and the following diagram is horizontally left adjointable, see
[
Cis20
, Prop. 7.1.14]
:

(1)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{w_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}[\underline{{S}}^{-1}]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(w_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{A}}})[w_{*}\underline{{S}}^{-1}]}}

Using the equivalence
(w_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{A}}})[w_{*}\underline{{S}}^{-1}]\simeq w_{*}(\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}[\underline{{S}}^{-1}])
(which can be verified fiberwise), we conclude that
\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}
has
w
-indexed coproducts and the localization preserves them.

Furthermore, the dual statement shows that if
\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}
admits
w
-indexed products that preserve
\underline{{S}}
, so does
\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}[\underline{{S}}^{-1}]
and the localization preserves them. In fact, if
\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}
is
G
-semiadditive, that
w
-indexed coproducts preserve
\underline{{S}}
implies that
w
-indexed products also do. In total, if
\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}
is
G
-semiadditive and
\underline{{S}}
is closed under
w
-indexed coproducts, then
\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}[\underline{{S}}^{-1}]
admits
w
-indexed products and coproducts and the localization functor preserves both of them. By naturality of the norm map
w_{!}\to w_{*}
along functors preserving
w
-(co)products, and by essential surjectivity of
\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}\to\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}[\underline{{S}}^{-1}]
, we deduce that
\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}[\underline{{S}}^{-1}]
is also
G
-semiadditive.

Lastly, the statement that
\overline{F}
preserves finite indexed coproducts is a straightforward consequence of the fact that the square
Equation

1
is horizontally left adjointable and that the vertical arrow
{w_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}}\rightarrow{(w_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{A}}})[w_{*}\underline{{S}}^{-1}]}
is essentially surjective.
∎

2.2.
Perfect
G
-stable categories and Karoubi sequences

We now recall the substrate on which our notion of equivariant motives will be built, namely, an equivariant generalization of
\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}
. The basic reference for these materials is
[
Hil26
, §2.5]
.

Recollections 2.2.1
.

We let
\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\subset\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}_{G}
be the nonfull
G
-subcategory of small
G
-stable categories which are idempotent-complete and
G
-exact functors. As in the nonequivariant setting, there is an equivalence

(2)

\mathrm{Ind}\colon\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\simeq\underline{{\mathrm{Pr}}}^{L}_{G,\mathrm{st},\omega}\penalty\mskip 6.0mu plus 1.0mu\mathpunct{}\nonscript\mkern-3.0mu{:}\mskip 2.0mu(-)^{\omega}

of
G
-categories, cf.
[
Hil26
, Nota. 2.1.38]
, where the right hand side is the nonfull
G
-subcategory of the
G
-category
\underline{{\mathrm{Pr}}}^{L}_{G,\mathrm{st}}
of
G
-presentable-stable categories spanned by the compactly-generated ones and compact-preserving functors. In fact, there are
G
-symmetric monoidal structures on both sides and this equivalence can be made compatible with these structures by
[
HJS
]
. Moreover, by
[
Hil26
, Thm. 2.5.11]
, the inclusion
\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\subset\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}_{G}
induces a nonfull inclusion

(3)

\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\subset\underline{{\mackey}}_{G}({\mathrm{Cat}}^{\mathrm{perf}})

which inherits all
G
-(co)limits.

Example 2.2.3

(Categories with actions)
.

Let
{\mathcal{C}}\in\mathrm{CAlg}(\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}})^{BG}
be an ordinary stably symmetric monoidal category with a
G
-action. Then
{\mathcal{C}}
induces a Borel
G
-stable
G
-category
\underline{{\mathrm{Bor}}}({\mathcal{C}})=\{G/H\mapsto{\mathcal{C}}^{hH}\}_{H\leq G}
, and it can be canonically promoted to a
G
-commutative algebra in
\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}
. This is because by
[
Hil26
, Thm. 2.4.10 (2)]
, the inclusion
\underline{{\mathrm{Bor}}}(\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}})\hookrightarrow\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}
refines to a
G
-lax symmetric monoidal functor. Then, by applying
\mathrm{CAlg}_{G}(-)
to this map and invoking
[
Hil26
, Thm. 2.4.10 (3)]
, we obtain an inclusion
\mathrm{CAlg}(\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}})^{BG}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{CAlg}_{G}(\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}})
.

Definition 2.2.4
.

A Karoubi sequence is a sequence
\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{B}}}\rightarrow\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}
in
\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}
whose composite is null and is both a fiber and a cofiber sequence in
\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}
.

Remark 2.2.5
.

Since the inclusion
Equation

3
inherits all
G
-(co)limits, in particular, it inherits the (co)fiber sequences in Mackey functors which in turn are computed pointwise by
[
Bar17
, Cor. 6.7.1]
. This allows us to port many of the standard results about Karoubi sequences in the nonequivariant context, for instance, as recorded in
[
CDH+23
, App. A]
. Furthermore, note that nullity of a map in
\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}
is a property, and so the definition above makes sense without having to specify a commuting square involving the zero functor.

The
G
-category
\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}
is amenable to isotropy separation methods which allows us to perform proofs by inducting on the size of the finite group
G
. We record these points now.

Construction 2.2.6
.

Let
\mathcal{F}
be a family of subgroups in

and writing

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{\underline{{E\mathcal{F}}}}\otimes\widetilde{\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}}=\underline{{\func}}_{*}(\underline{{\widetilde{E\mathcal{F}}}},\underline{{\widetilde{{\mathcal{C}}}}})}

It will be convenient to use the suggestive notation

Observation 2.2.7
.

Let
\mathcal{P}
be the family of proper subgroups. We may use this family to perform isotropy separations in an arbitrary
G
-stable presentable category as follows: let
\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}\in\mathrm{Pr}^{L}_{G,\mathrm{st}}
and
x\in\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}
. Then
x=0
if and only if for all
H\lneq G
,
\res^{G}_{H}x=0\in\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}(G/H)
and
\Phi^{\mathcal{P}}x=0\in\Phi^{\mathcal{P}}\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}\in\mathrm{Pr}^{L}_{\mathrm{st}}
. The forwards implication is clear and to see the converse, we consider the cofiber sequence

E\mathcal{P}_{+}\otimes x\longrightarrow x\longrightarrow\widetilde{E\mathcal{P}}\otimes x
in
\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}
where
\widetilde{E\mathcal{P}}\otimes x
is the image of
\Phi^{\mathcal{P}}x
under the inclusion
\Phi^{\mathcal{P}}\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}\subseteq\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}
. Since
\Phi^{\mathcal{P}}x=0
, the map
E\mathcal{P}_{+}\otimes x\rightarrow x
is an equivalence. On the other hand,
E\mathcal{P}_{+}\otimes x
is in the image of the inclusion
\underline{{\func}}(\underline{{E\mathcal{P}}},\underline{{E}})\subseteq\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}
. Since
\coprod_{H\lneq G}G/H\rightarrow E\mathcal{P}
is an effective epimorphism, checking that
E\mathcal{P}_{+}\otimes x\in\underline{{\func}}(\underline{{E\mathcal{P}}},\underline{{\mathcal{E}}})
is zero is equivalent to checking that
x
goes to zero under the restriction
{\func}_{G}(\underline{{E\mathcal{P}}},\underline{{\mathcal{E}}})\rightarrow\func_{G}(G/H,\underline{{\mathcal{E}}})\simeq\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}(G/H)
. But this is precisely supplied by the hypothesis that
\res^{G}_{H}x=0
.

2.3.
Isotropy separation for fully faithfulness

A the key point in our work is an analysis to prove fully faithfulness of certain functors. In this subsection, we provide a tool to detect fully faithfulness of
G
-exact functors between
G
-stable
G
-categories. We do this by isotropy separation in the
G
-category of
G
-stable
G
-categories. Since this
G
-category is itself not
G
-stable, isotropy separation methods do not come “for free”.

where we have also used that
{E\mathcal{F}}_{+}\otimes Fy\simeq F({E\mathcal{F}}_{+}\otimes y)
and
\widetilde{E\mathcal{F}}\otimes Fy\simeq F(\widetilde{E\mathcal{F}}\otimes y)
since
F\colon\widetilde{\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}}\rightarrow\widetilde{\underline{{{\mathcal{D}}}}}
preserves parametrized colimits. By hypothesis, the left vertical map is an equivalence.

Recall by definition that
\Phi^{\mathcal{F}}\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}\coloneqq(\Phi^{\mathcal{F}}\widetilde{\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}})^{\omega}
and similarly for
\underline{{{\mathcal{D}}}}
. Hence, since the functor

is an equivalence if and only if the right vertical map in
Equation

5
is an equivalence if and only if the middle vertical map of

We will also need the following fact for our analysis.

Lemma 2.3.2
.

Let
F\colon\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}\rightarrow\underline{{{\mathcal{D}}}}
be a fully faithful morphism in
\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{W}
. Then
w_{\otimes}F\colon w_{\otimes}\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}\rightarrow w_{\otimes}\underline{{{\mathcal{D}}}}
is a fully faithful morphism in
\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{V}
.

Proof.

By the
G
-symmetric monoidal equivalence
\mathrm{Ind}\colon\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\rightleftharpoons\underline{{\mathrm{Pr}}}^{L}_{\mathrm{st},\omega}\penalty\mskip 6.0mu plus 1.0mu\mathpunct{}\nonscript\mkern-3.0mu{:}\mskip 2.0mu(-)^{\omega}
, we see that
\mathrm{Ind}(w_{\otimes}F)\colon\mathrm{Ind}(w_{\otimes}\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}})\rightarrow\mathrm{Ind}(w_{\otimes}\underline{{{\mathcal{D}}}})
identifies with
w_{\otimes}\mathrm{Ind}F\colon w_{\otimes}\mathrm{Ind}\underline{{{\mathcal{C}}}}\rightarrow w_{\otimes}\mathrm{Ind}\underline{{{\mathcal{D}}}}
. Hence, it suffices to prove that
w_{\otimes}\mathrm{Ind}F
is fully faithful.

Now,
\mathrm{Ind}F
is fully faithful by hypothesis, and it admits a right adjoint
R
which is also in
\mathrm{Pr}^{L}_{W,\mathrm{st}}
. In particular, the unit map
\mathrm{id}\to R\circ\mathrm{Ind}F
is an equivalence, and induces, by
2
-functoriality of
w_{\otimes}
from
D.0.4
, an equivalence
\mathrm{id}\to w_{\otimes}R\circ w_{\otimes}\mathrm{Ind}F
. Again by
2
-functoriality of
w_{\otimes}
, this equivalence is the unit of an adjunction
w_{\otimes}\mathrm{Ind}F\dashv w_{\otimes}R
, and so we conclude that
w_{\otimes}\mathrm{Ind}F
is fully faithful, as was to be shown.
∎

3.
Equivariant localizing motives

3.1.
Definitions and constructions

The goal of this section is to define
G
-localizing motives, following the perspective from
[
RSW25
]
, and prove
3.1.13
.

Definition 3.1.1
.

A
G
-localizing invariant
is a
G
-semiadditive functor
E\colon\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\to\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}
, where
\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}
is some
G
-stable
G
-category, such that
E_{H}\colon{\mathrm{Cat}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{H}\to{\mathcal{E}}_{H}
sends Karoubi sequences to bifiber sequences for every subgroup
H\leq G
. More generally, for
V
a finite
G
-set, a
V
-localizing invariant
is a
V
-semiadditive functor
E\colon\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{V}\to\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}
where
\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}
is some
V
-stable
V
-category, and which sends fiberwise Karoubi sequences to levelwise bifiber sequences.

A
G
- or more generally
V
-localizing invariant is said to be
finitary
if it also preserves fiberwise filtered colimits. We denote by
\underline{{\func}}^{\mathrm{fin.loc.}}(\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G},\underline{{\mathcal{E}}})
the full
G
-subcategory of
\underline{{\func}}(\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G},\underline{{\mathcal{E}}})
which at level
H\leq G
consists of the finitary
H
-localizing invariants.

The following is the ur-example that the above notions are supposed to axiomatize:

Definition 3.1.4
.

A map
\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}\to\underline{{\mathcal{B}}}
in
\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}
is called a
motivic equivalence
if it is sent to an equivalence by every finitary
G
-localizing invariant. We also have an analogous notion of motivic equivalences in
\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{V}
for any finite
G
-set

. We let
\underline{{W}}_{\mathrm{mot}}
denote the

-subcategory of

-motivic equivalences, whose

-fixed points is the category of

To see that
\underline{{W}}_{\mathrm{mot}}
is well-defined, we need the following verification:

Lemma 3.1.5
.

\underline{{W}}_{\mathrm{mot}}
does define a
G
-subcategory of
\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}
, i.e. restrictions of
G
-motivic equivalences are
H
-motivic equivalences, for every subgroup
H\leq G
. More generally, for any map
w:W\to V
of finite
G
-sets,
w^{*}
sends motivic equivalences of
V
-stable
V
-categories to motivic equivalences of
W
-stable
W
-categories.

Proof.

Given any
H
-localizing invariant
E:\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{H}\to\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}
, by adjunction we get a
G
-functor
\coind_{H}^{G}E\colon\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\to\coind_{H}^{G}\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}
. Note that if
E
is finitary, then so is
\coind_{H}^{G}E
by
2.1.16
. We claim now that
\coind_{H}^{G}E
is a
G
-localizing invariant.

First, we note that it is clearly
G
-semiadditive if
E
was
H
-semiadditive since
\coind^{G}_{H}E
may be written as the composite

\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\xlongrightarrow{\eta}\coind^{G}_{H}\res^{G}_{H}\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}=\coind^{G}_{H}\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{H}\xlongrightarrow{\coind^{G}_{H}E}\coind^{G}_{H}\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}

and both maps preserve finite indexed products.

For
f:\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}\to\underline{{\mathcal{B}}}
a
G
-exact functor of
G
-stable
G
-categories, and
K\leq G
a subgroup,
\coind_{H}^{G}E(f)^{K}\in(\coind_{H}^{G}\underline{{\mathcal{E}}})^{K}\simeq\prod_{r\in H\backslash G/K}\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}^{H\cap K^{r}}
is given by the family of the
E^{H\cap K^{r}}(\res_{H\cap K^{r}}^{G}f)
. From this the claim follows directly because restrictions of fiberwise Karoubi sequences are (by definition!) fiberwise Karoubi sequences. Now if
f
is a
G
-motivic equivalence, the above family is an equivalence and hence plugging in subgroups

of

is an equivalence, and so

is an
H
-motivic equivalence.
∎

With this, we can now use Dwyer–Kan localizations to define equivariant localizing motives.

Definition 3.1.6
.

We let
\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G}:=\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}[\underline{{W}}^{-1}_{\mathrm{mot}}]
denote the
G
-category of
G
-localizing motives
, and we let
\underline{{\mathcal{U}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G}:\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\to\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G}
denote the induced localization functor. More generally, for a finite
G
-set
V
, we have similarly
\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{V}
and
\underline{{\mathcal{U}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{V}
.

Remark 3.1.7
.

Let us briefly discuss the role of the adjective “finitary” in the definion above. One could perfectly have defined all relevant notions here without this adjective, and in fact our proof ultimately works also in the context of non-finitary localizing motives.

The first role this adjective plays is an a priori size control: it is easier to show that the localization at “finitary motivic equivalences” is actually a locally small category than to show the same statement for the localization at “absolute motivic equivalences”, though the latter is also true. This would maybe justify considering
\kappa
-finitary localizing invariants for arbitrary regular cardinals
\kappa
, rather than specifically
\kappa=\aleph_{0}
– again, our arguments carry over to this setting with no change.

However, the point of restricting to
\kappa=\aleph_{0}
is that for
\kappa>\aleph_{1}
, the relevant category of motives seems much harder to access, and in particular it seems difficult to say anything nontrivial about it, while for
\kappa=\aleph_{1}
, it turns out (miraculously) to agree with the case of
\kappa=\aleph_{0}
, see
[
RSW25
, Thm. 1.8]
. Since virtually every localizing invariant one encounters is
\aleph_{1}
-finitary, the restriction to this version of localizing motives seems completely mild, and we work in this setting for convenience and in order to avoid overloading our statements with set-theoretic considerations.

Before we go on, we make a small observation that will be useful throughout. Namely, we defined motivic equivalences in terms of
G
-localizing invariants, which are certain
G
-functors, and staring at the bare category
{\mathrm{Cat}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}
, it may not be clear what these correspond to without remembering all the
G
-structure. We now work towards proving
3.1.12
that we can also do away with some of the “
G
” in this definition. This will be convenient for some proofs.

Lemma 3.1.8
.

Let
E:{\mathrm{Cat}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\to\mathcal{E}
be an additive functor to a stable category sending Karoubi sequences to bifiber sequences. The
G
-semiadditive
G
-functor
\widetilde{E}:\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\to\underline{{\mackey}}_{G}(\mathcal{E})
corresponding to
E
under the adjunction from
2.1.12
is a
G
-localizing invariant. If
E
preserves filtered colimits, then
\tilde{E}
preserves fiberwise filtered colimits. More generally, the statement holds when we replace
G
by a finite
G
-set
V
.

Proof.

For fixed subgroups
K\leq H\leq G
, using the description of the unit and the counit from
2.1.12
, we find that the composite
\widetilde{E}^{H}:\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{ex}}_{H}\to\mackey_{H}(\mathcal{E})\xrightarrow{(-)^{K}}\mathcal{E}
is given by
E(\mathrm{Ind}_{K}^{G}\res_{K}^{H}-)
, which clearly sends Karoubi sequences to bifiber sequences if
E
does. The filtered colimits claim also follows from that analysis.
∎

Definition 3.1.9
.

A
Mackey
G
-localizing invariant
is an additive functor
E:{\mathrm{Cat}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\to\mathcal{E}
to some stable category
\mathcal{E}
sending Karoubi sequences to bifiber sequences. It is finitary if it sends filtered colimits to filtered colimits. A
Mackey motivic equivalence
is a
G
-exact functor
\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}\to\underline{{\mathcal{B}}}
between small
G
-stable
G
-categories that is sent to an equivalence by every finitary Mackey
G
-localizing invariant. We have analogous definitions for finite
G
-sets
V
.

Definition 3.1.10
.

Ordinary (non-connective, algebraic)
K
-theory of
G
-fixed points evidently gives a Mackey
G
-localizing invariant
K((-)^{G}):\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\to\mathrm{Sp}
. We define equivariant
K
-theory
\underline{{K}}_{G}
to be the
G
-localizing invariant associated to it as in
3.1.8
.

Observation 3.1.11
.

The combination of
2.1.12
and
3.1.8
essentially states that (finitary) Mackey
G
-localizing invariants are a special case of
G
-localizing invariants, namely the special case where the target
\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}
is
11
11

11

We do not believe that this is a property, rather it seems to be extra structure on
\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}
to witness it as such.
of the form
\underline{{\mackey}}_{G}(\mathcal{E}_{0})
for some
\mathcal{E}_{0}
.

Corollary 3.1.12
.

Motivic equivalences and Mackey motivic equivalences agree.

Proof.

By
3.1.8
, we find that every finitary Mackey
G
-localizing invariant
E:{\mathrm{Cat}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\to\mathcal{E}
gives rise to a finitary
G
-localizing invariant
\widetilde{\mathcal{E}}:\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\to\underline{{\mackey}}_{G}(\mathcal{E})
, and
E
can be recovered as the composite
{\mathrm{Cat}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\xrightarrow{\widetilde{E}^{G}}\mackey_{G}(\mathcal{E})\xrightarrow{(-)^{G}}\mathcal{E}

This directly implies that motivic equivalences are Mackey motivic equivalences. Conversely, a finitary
G
-localizing invariant
\underline{{E}}:\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\to\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}
gives rise to a Mackey localizing invariant
E_{G}:{\mathrm{Cat}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\to\mathcal{E}_{G}
upon taking
G
-fixed points, and hence Mackey motivic equivalences are also motivic equivalences.
∎

Now as in
[
RSW25
]
, and based on

, we find:

Theorem 3.1.13
.

The fiberwise localization
\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\to\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G}
is the universal finitary
G
-localizing invariant. More precisely,
\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G}
is
G
-presentable and
G
-stable, and for any
G
-presentable
G
-stable
G
-category
\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}
, restriction along this localization

(\underline{{{\mathcal{U}}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G})^{*}\colon\underline{{\func}}^{L}(\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G},\underline{{\mathcal{E}}})\xlongrightarrow{\simeq}\underline{{\func}}^{\mathrm{fin.loc.}}(\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G},\underline{{\mathcal{E}}})

is an equivalence. More generally, for any finite
G
-set

, the localization
\underline{{{\mathcal{U}}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{V}\colon\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{V}\to\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{V}
witnesses the target as the universal finitary

-localizing invariant.

Thus,
\underline{{{\mathcal{U}}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G}\colon\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G}
admits another universal property apart from the tautological one as the initial functor which inverts motivic equivalences. This is analogous to the main result of
[
RSW25
]
and shows that the localization of
\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}
at motivic equivalences satisfies a Blumberg–Gepner–Tabuada-style universal property
[
BGT13
]
, that is, a universal property among presentable
G
-categories equipped with a finitary
G
-localizing invariant.

Proof of
3.1.13
.

We first show that
\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G}
is
G
-semiadditive, and that the localization functor
\underline{{{\mathcal{U}}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G}
is
G
-semiadditive as well. By
2.1.23
, it suffices to show that induction
\mathrm{Ind}_{H}^{K}:\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{H}\to\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{K}
preserves motivic equivalences for all subgroups
H\leq K\leq G
. By
3.1.12
, it suffices to show that it preserves Mackey motivic equivalences, which is evident since it is finitary and preserves Karoubi sequences.

Next, we argue that
\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G}
is
G
-presentable and
G
-stable, and that
\underline{{{\mathcal{U}}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G}
is a finitary
G
-localizing invariant. For
G
-presentable-stability, since we already know that
\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G}
is
G
-semiadditive (which in particular means that the restriction functorialities preserve ordinary colimits), it thus suffices by
[
Hil24
, Thm. 6.1.2 (7)]
to show that
\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G}
is fiberwise stable and presentable. By
B.0.1
and
B.0.4
, the localization in question is fiberwise
equivalent to the localization of
\mathrm{Mod}_{\mathrm{Sp}_{H}^{\omega}}(\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}})
at
\mathrm{Sp}_{H}^{\omega}
-motivic equivalences in the sense of
[
RSW25
, App. B]
. Therefore, by
[
RSW25
, Thm. B.6 and Rmk. B.11]
, it is fiberwise presentable and stable, and the localization functor
\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{H}\to\mathrm{Cat}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{H}[W_{\mathrm{mot},H}^{-1}]
is a finitary Mackey
H
-localizing invariant. Hence, together the localization functors assemble into a finitary
G
-localizing invariant
\underline{{{\mathcal{U}}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G}
.

Finally, we show the universal property. By construction, we have a fully faithful functor
(\underline{{\mathcal{U}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G})^{*}\colon\underline{{\func}}^{L}(\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G},\underline{{\mathcal{E}}})\hookrightarrow\underline{{\func}}(\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G},\underline{{\mathcal{E}}})
. This in fact lands in the full subcategory of finitary
G
-localizing invariants since
\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G}
was itself a
G
-localizing invariant by the previous paragraph. To see that this is essentially surjective on finitary
G
-localizing invariants
E\colon\underline{{\mathrm{Cat}}}^{\mathrm{perf}}_{G}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}
, first note that any such functor will in particular invert the motivic equivalences by definition, and therefore it factors uniquely through a functor
\overline{E}\colon\underline{{\mathrm{Mot}}}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{G}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{E}}}
. It remains to show that
\overline{E}
preserves
G
-colimits. By
2.1.23
, we know at least that it preserves finite indexed coproducts. On the other hand, by the previous paragraph and again
[
RSW25
, Thm. B.6]
,
\overline{E}
also preserves fiberwise colimits. Hence,
\overline{E}
preserves arbitrary
G
-colimits, as required.
∎

We end this subsection by making contact with recent breakthroughs in K-theory. A remarkable result of Efimov

Corollary 3.1.14

The category

is a rigid commutative algebra in

, as well as as a commutative algebra over

, equivalently,

12

See

]
for a definition of rigidity in arbitrary symmetric monoidal
2
-categories.
in
\mathrm{Pr}^{L}_{G,\mathrm{st}}
.

Proof.

The proof of

shows that

is equivalent to
